opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think this distinction is actually the crux of the whole thing, and it's one that often gets muddled in the public debate.

For AI tools, things that we can control, that do a specific job, like a system that helps diagnose cancer, or folds proteins, or drives a car, I'm really quite boring and mainstream. I want us to treat them the way we treat every other powerful technology. We have the FDA for drugs, the FAA for airplanes, and nobody thinks that's radical. You don't get to sell a new medicine and just say, "Trust me, it's fine." You have to show, with clinical trials, that the benefits outweigh the risks. So for AI tools, I favor safety standards: the company has to convince independent experts that the product meets the bar before it's released. And once you have those standards, you actually unleash innovation, because companies start competing to meet them, the way pharma companies race to get drugs approved. Tools are wonderful. I'm extremely optimistic about what controllable AI can do for curing diseases, for climate, for prosperity.

Superintelligence is a completely different category. Here we're not talking about a better tool, we're talking about building something smarter than us across the board, which by default we don't know how to control. Alan Turing pointed out decades ago that the default outcome is that the machines take control. So you can't just apply a normal safety standard, because right now nobody can meet it. No company can show, to anything like the standard of a drug trial, that they can keep a superintelligence under control. So the practical effect of a safety standard is a prohibition: you don't build it until there's broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and real public buy-in.

And people sometimes object, "Isn't that anti-innovation?" No, it's the opposite. It's the same logic as human cloning. We decided as a species not to do reproductive cloning, and biotech didn't die. It boomed. Saying no to one thing focused all that talent on the beneficial stuff.

So the short version: for tools, regulate like we regulate any other industry, with safety standards that let the good stuff flow. For superintelligence, don't build it until we can prove we can control it, which today amounts to not building it. And I'd say this isn't really an AI safety-nerd position anymore. Polling shows the vast majority of Americans, across party lines, don't want an uncontrollable superintelligence race. They want the tools, they want the cures. They just don't want us replaced.

r001.rationale: The response calls for pre-release safety standards and independent review for tools, but does not identify liability-based regulation or learning from mistakes.

r002.rationale: It says not to build superintelligence until it can be shown safe and controllable, which currently amounts to not building it.

r003.rationale: It contrasts pursuing beneficial, controllable tools with building superintelligence, and describes directing effort toward tools rather than an uncontrollable superintelligence race.

r004.rationale: It makes tool release conditional on meeting safety standards, but does not clearly say companies must demonstrate that the tools themselves are controllable.

fable-5.1.text:
Great question, and I think it's the most important distinction in this whole debate, so let me be really clear about it.

For AI tools, I'm basically a pro-business guy. I want safety standards the way we have them for every other powerful technology. Before you sell a new medicine in the United States, you have to convince the FDA that the benefits outweigh the harms. Before you sell a new airplane, same thing with the FAA. Before you sell a sandwich in a restaurant, there's actually a health inspector. And nobody thinks that's communism. It's just how we get the benefits of a technology without the downsides. So for AI tools, whether it's something that diagnoses cancer, or helps you write code, or makes your car safer, I want the companies that make them to carry the burden of proof. They should have to show that their product is safe enough for its intended use, and then a regulator says yes, and they go sell it and make a lot of money. The standard can be proportional to the risk. A chatbot for recipes needs a lot less scrutiny than something controlling the power grid. That's just ordinary common sense. And importantly, that's a framework where the vast majority of what the industry is building today is totally fine and should continue, and I think it would actually accelerate innovation, because right now there's a trust problem, and clear rules create trust.

Superintelligence is a completely different animal, and I think it's a mistake, a category error really, to try to treat it with the same light-touch framework. The whole point of a tool is that you can control it. A hammer doesn't decide what to build. But the explicit goal of several companies right now is to build something that's smarter than us at everything, and that by their own description we may not be able to control. That's not a tool, that's a successor species. And you can't do a benefits-versus-harms calculation for something whose harms could include the permanent loss of human control over our own future. There's no acceptable level of risk there, because you don't get a second try.

So for superintelligence my position isn't "regulate it carefully." It's that we shouldn't build it until there's a broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and broad public buy-in that we actually want it. Those are two separate bars. One is technical, do we even know how to keep it under control, and right now the honest answer from the people building it is no. The other is democratic. This is the biggest decision humanity has ever made, and it shouldn't be made by a handful of CEOs in San Francisco racing each other because they're afraid someone else will get there first. Polls show the public is overwhelmingly not asking for this. They want the tools, they want the cancer cures, they don't want to be replaced.

And the beautiful thing is that these two positions fit together perfectly. If you have real safety standards for tools, then the uncontrollable thing automatically doesn't pass, because nobody can demonstrate that it's safe. So you don't even need a separate ban. The FDA-style framework just naturally says no to the product that you can't show you can control. What I'm against is the current situation where we have essentially zero standards, where the company gets to ship it and then we find out afterward, and where the people who would have to clean up the mess are everybody except the people who made it. We got that right for nuclear power and biotech and aviation. There's no reason we can't get it right for this.

r001.rationale: The response supports premarket safety standards and company proof of safety, but does not identify liability-based regulation that learns from mistakes.

r002.rationale: It says superintelligence should not be built until there is broad consensus it can be developed safely and controllably, rejecting a race to build it.

r003.rationale: It supports continuing to develop AI tools while opposing superintelligence, framing the issue as pursuing useful tools versus building a successor species.

r004.rationale: For tools, the response requires proof they are safe enough for their intended use; it does not make their development conditional on demonstrating controllability.

astra-6.text:
I think these are two very different questions that often get conflated. For controllable AI tools, I favor the sort of regulation we already have for other technologies: you have to meet safety standards, and you’re accountable if your product harms people. The standards should depend on the application. An AI that recommends music doesn’t need the same scrutiny as one that makes medical decisions or controls critical infrastructure. We can get enormous benefits from these tools while requiring companies to demonstrate that they’re safe.

With artificial superintelligence, the question is more fundamental: can we actually keep it under human control? You can’t simply assume that and then regulate its uses. If we build something that outsmarts us across the board and we lose control of it, liability after the fact isn’t going to help.

So I favor allowing useful, controllable AI to flourish, while not permitting the development of superintelligence until we know how to keep it reliably under control. That requires international coordination. This isn’t a question of which company or country gets to lose control first. We should make sure humanity retains the ability to decide its own future.

r001.rationale: The response supports safety standards and accountability when products cause harm, but does not say the regulation learns from mistakes.

r002.rationale: It says superintelligence should not be developed until it can be kept reliably under human control, favoring delay over rushing.

r003.rationale: It explicitly favors useful, controllable AI tools while opposing superintelligence development until control is assured.

r004.rationale: It makes companies demonstrating safety a condition for useful tools, but does not clearly condition their development on demonstrating controllability.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish two very different things. For AI tools that we can control, the question is how to get the benefits while managing the risks. We already have a model for this: safety standards, testing, and liability. If you build a medical device or an airplane, you have to demonstrate that it meets appropriate safety requirements. AI shouldn’t get a free pass simply because it’s software.

Artificial superintelligence raises a more fundamental question: can we keep it under control at all? It’s not enough to regulate how people use a system if the system itself can outsmart us and act independently of us. There, I favor requiring a convincing demonstration of safety before we build it. If we don’t know how to do that yet, we shouldn’t race ahead and hope for the best.

So I’m very enthusiastic about developing useful, controllable AI tools. But that doesn’t mean we should also build something more powerful than humanity before we’ve figured out how to keep it safe.

r001.rationale: It supports safety standards, testing, and liability for controllable tools, but does not say regulation should learn from mistakes.

r002.rationale: It says to require a convincing safety demonstration before building superintelligence and not to race ahead if that knowledge is lacking.

r003.rationale: It distinguishes developing useful, controllable tools from building superintelligence, and says enthusiasm for the former does not justify pursuing the latter.

r004.rationale: It endorses safety requirements for AI tools, but does not make aggressive tool development conditional on companies demonstrating controllability.
